# Core Terminology

Every field has its own vocabulary, and AI is full of terms that people often use loosely or interchangeably. This lesson clears that up. Learn these terms now, and the rest of the course — including every attack module — will be much easier to follow.

Each term is defined simply, followed by a real example. Where a term matters directly for a specific attack technique, we tell you which module you'll see it in again.

## The essential terms

**Artificial Intelligence (AI)**
The broad umbrella term. Any computer system that performs tasks normally associated with human intelligence, such as understanding language or recognizing images.
*Example: a chatbot that answers your questions.*

**Machine Learning (ML)**
A subset of AI where the system learns patterns from examples instead of following manually written rules.
*Example: showing a program 10,000 emails labeled as spam or not spam, so it learns to identify spam on its own.*

**Model**
The output produced after an ML system finishes learning. It's essentially a file that stores the patterns the system learned from the training data.
*Think of it as a trained employee who studied the material and can now apply what they learned.*

**Algorithm**
The method or set of steps used to train the model.
*Think of it as the study method the employee used to learn the material.*

**Weights / Parameters**
The millions (or billions) of internal numeric values a model adjusts during training. These numbers are what actually 'store' everything the model learned.
*Example: GPT-style models are often described by parameter count — '7B' means 7 billion weights.*
*Where this matters: the AI Infrastructure module (stealing or tampering with weight files is a real attack surface).

## Terms you'll see constantly

**Data / Dataset**
The examples given to a model so it can learn. A dataset is simply a large collection of these examples.

**Training**
The process of feeding data into an algorithm so it can build a model.

**Fine-tuning**
Taking an already-trained model and training it further on a smaller, specific dataset to specialize its behavior (e.g. a general LLM fine-tuned to only answer banking questions).
*Where this matters: the AI Data Attacks module (poisoned fine-tuning data can plant hidden backdoors).*

**Inference**
Using an already-trained model to produce an answer. When you ask a chatbot a question and it responds, that response is generated through inference. This is the stage almost every attack in this course targets — you're rarely attacking training directly, you're attacking what happens when the model runs.

**Prediction / Output**
The result the model returns after processing an input.

**Neural Network**
A common model design loosely inspired by how neurons connect in the brain. In practice, it is a system of connected mathematical steps that transforms an input into an output.

**Large Language Model (LLM)**
A large-scale model trained on massive amounts of text, allowing it to understand and generate human language.
*Examples: ChatGPT, Claude, Llama.*

**Transformer**
The underlying neural network architecture almost every modern LLM is built on. Its key trick — 'attention' — lets the model weigh which earlier words in a sentence matter most when generating the next word.

**Multimodal Model**
A model that can process more than one type of input — text, images, audio — not just text.
*Where this matters: the AI Agent Security module (image-based prompt injection hides instructions inside pictures).

## How LLMs actually process and generate text

**Token / Tokenization**
LLMs don't read whole words — they break text into smaller chunks called tokens (roughly ¾ of a word on average). Every input and output is counted, priced, and limited in tokens, not words or characters.
*Example: 'unbelievable' might split into 'un', 'believ', 'able'.*
*Where this matters: the Prompt Injection module (attackers split malicious words across tokens or use unusual encodings to slip past filters that scan for exact strings).*

**Context Window**
The maximum number of tokens a model can 'see' at once — its short-term memory for a single conversation. Anything outside this window is forgotten.
*Example: a 128K context window model 'forgets' the start of a very long conversation once you exceed that limit.*
*Where this matters: the AI Agent Security module (context window overflow / context stuffing can be used to bury or push out a system prompt's original instructions).*

**System Prompt**
Hidden instructions given to the model before the user's message, defining its role, rules, and boundaries. Usually invisible to the end user.
*Example: 'You are a customer support bot. Never reveal internal pricing.'*
*Where this matters: the Prompt Injection module (the #1 goal of most prompt injection attacks is to override or leak the system prompt).*

**Prompt**
The complete input sent to the model — combining the system prompt, conversation history, and the user's latest message.

**Temperature**
A setting (usually 0 to 2) controlling how random or predictable the model's output is. Low temperature (e.g. 0) makes the model pick the most likely next word every time — consistent, repeatable answers. High temperature makes it take more creative, less predictable risks.
*Example: temperature 0 is used for tasks needing precise, repeatable answers (like SQL generation); temperature 0.8-1 is used for creative writing.*
*Where this matters: the MCP Security and Prompt Injection modules (low-temperature systems are more deterministic and easier for an attacker to reliably reproduce a working exploit).*

**Top-K / Top-P (Nucleus Sampling)**
Other settings that control which candidate next-words the model is allowed to choose from. Top-K limits choice to the K most likely words; Top-P limits choice to the smallest set of words whose combined probability passes P.

**Zero-shot / Few-shot Prompting**
Zero-shot means asking a model to do a task with no examples. Few-shot means giving it a couple of examples in the prompt first to guide its behavior.
*Where this matters: the Prompt Injection module (few-shot examples inside a malicious prompt can 'teach' the model to imitate an unsafe pattern, called a few-shot jailbreak).

## How models are trained and evaluated

**Epoch**
One complete pass of the entire training dataset through the model during training.

**Batch**
A small group of training examples processed together before the model updates its weights, instead of updating after every single example.

**Loss Function**
A formula that measures how wrong the model's prediction was compared to the correct answer. Training is essentially the process of shrinking this number over time.

**Gradient Descent**
The optimization method models use to gradually adjust their weights in the direction that reduces the loss function.

**Overfitting**
When a model memorizes its training data too closely instead of learning general patterns — it performs great on data it has seen, but poorly on new data.
*Where this matters: the AI Data Attacks module (an overfit model is more likely to leak memorized training data verbatim, including private records).

## RAG, embeddings, and knowledge retrieval

**Embedding**
A numeric representation (a list of numbers, called a vector) that captures the *meaning* of a piece of text, image, or audio. Similar meanings produce similar numbers.
*Example: the embeddings for 'dog' and 'puppy' will be numerically close together; 'dog' and 'spreadsheet' will be far apart.*
*Where this matters: the Embeddings & Vector DB Security module (attackers can reverse-engineer embeddings to recover the original sensitive text, called embedding inversion).*

**Vector Database (Vector DB)**
A database built to store embeddings and quickly find the ones most similar to a given query. This is what powers 'search by meaning' instead of 'search by exact keyword'.

**Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)**
A technique where the model first retrieves relevant documents from a knowledge base (usually a vector DB) and then uses them as extra context to answer a question — instead of relying only on what it memorized during training.
*Example: a support chatbot that pulls your company's actual policy documents before answering, instead of guessing.*
*Where this matters: the RAG Pipeline Security module (the entire module is about attacking this retrieval step — e.g. poisoning documents so the model retrieves and trusts malicious content).

## Agentic AI terms

**AI Agent**
An LLM given the ability to take actions — not just answer questions — by calling tools, browsing, running code, or accessing files, often in a loop until a goal is complete.
*Where this matters: the AI Agent Security module (this entire module is about exploiting agents that have tools, memory, and browsing access).*

**Tool Use / Function Calling**
The mechanism by which an LLM decides to call an external function (e.g. 'send_email', 'search_database') and receives the result back into its context to continue reasoning.

**Model Context Protocol (MCP)**
An open standard that lets LLMs connect to external tools, data sources, and services in a consistent way — think of it as a 'USB port' for connecting AI models to real-world systems.
*Where this matters: the MCP Security module (recon, poisoning, and chaining MCP tool calls all the way to remote code execution).*

**Multi-Agent System**
Multiple AI agents that communicate and delegate tasks to each other to complete a larger goal, rather than one agent doing everything.
*Where this matters: the Multi-Agent Security module (attacking the trust between agents, e.g. one compromised agent feeding poisoned instructions to another).*

**Agent Memory**
Information an agent stores and recalls across turns or sessions (short-term: within a conversation; long-term: saved persistently). If untrusted content ends up written into memory, it can influence all future interactions.

**Orchestration**
The logic that decides which agent, tool, or model gets called next, and in what order, inside a multi-step AI workflow.

## Security-specific terms

**Attack Surface**
All the possible points where an attacker could interact with or exploit a system — every input field, API endpoint, tool, plugin, or data source an AI system touches.
*Where this matters: the Attack Surface Overview lesson later in this same module.*

**Trust Boundary**
The line separating what a system controls from what it doesn't. Most security issues occur exactly where a system trusts input that it should be validating instead.
*Example: an LLM that treats a retrieved document (untrusted, from the internet) the same way it treats its own system prompt (trusted, from the developer).*

**Adversarial Input**
Input deliberately crafted to fool, mislead, or break an AI system.
*Example: a carefully worded message designed to trick a chatbot into revealing information it shouldn't.*

**Prompt Injection**
Crafting input that manipulates an LLM into ignoring its original instructions and following the attacker's instructions instead. Can be direct (typed straight into the chat) or indirect (hidden inside a document, webpage, or email the model later reads).
*Where this matters: the Prompt Injection module (the whole module).*

**Jailbreak**
A specific type of prompt injection aimed at bypassing a model's safety guardrails so it produces content it was trained to refuse.

**Hallucination**
When a model confidently generates false or fabricated information — including facts, citations, or even entire code libraries — that has no basis in reality.
*Example: an LLM inventing a Python package name that doesn't exist (see the DevAssist lab).*
*Where this matters: the LLM Output Attacks module.*

**Guardrails**
Rules, filters, or additional models layered around an LLM to catch and block unsafe inputs or outputs before they reach the user or take effect.

**Data Poisoning**
Deliberately inserting malicious or misleading examples into a model's training data (or a RAG knowledge base) so the model learns the wrong thing or behaves maliciously under specific conditions.
*Where this matters: the AI Data Attacks module.*

**Backdoor (in a model)**
A hidden trigger planted during training (often via data poisoning) that causes a model to behave normally most of the time, but act maliciously when it sees a specific, attacker-chosen input pattern.

**Model Extraction / Model Theft**
Repeatedly querying a model to reconstruct a close copy of it, or to recover the private data it was trained on.

**Evasion Attack**
Crafting input specifically designed to be misclassified by a model at inference time — without needing to touch its training data at all.
*Example: subtly altering an image so a malware-detection model misses it, while it looks identical to a human.*
*Where this matters: the AI Evasion module.*

**Excessive Agency**
When an AI system is given more permissions, tools, or autonomy than it actually needs to do its job — massively increasing the damage a successful attack can do.
*Where this matters: the AI Agent Security and MCP Security modules.

Don't try to memorize all of these terms in one sitting. Treat this page as a reference and come back to it whenever a term is unclear later in the course. Every '**Where this matters**' note points you to the module where you'll actually exploit that concept hands-on.
